newsitem.title: FRANCE: French police clash with anti-Front marchers.
newsitem.headline: French police clash with anti-Front marchers.

text.p: French riot police clashed on Tuesday with demonstrators in the Mediterranean port of Marseille protesting at a visit by extreme-right National Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen.
Police fired tear gas and detained about 20 protesters who hurled bottles and rubbish bins near where Le Pen was meeting the newly-elected National Front mayor of the southern town of Vitrolles.
Several people, including two police officers and an actor, Richard Martin, were slightly hurt during the clashes.

Police said up to 6,000 people, carrying a banner proclaiming "Racism, fascism: danger for democracy" marched through the city. Organisers, including unions and leftist parties, put the number at 10,000.
Clashes broke out when police blocked the marchers' path as they drew close to the building where Le Pen was meeting h Vitrolles mayor Catherine Megret and her husband, Bruno, the Front's number two.
Organisers urged the marchers to disperse but between 200 and 300 people pushed through police barriers.

Sporadic clashes later erupted in other parts of the city but police said the situation was under control by about 2200 GMT. A photographer said police shoved him to the ground and stripped him of his cameras.
The photographer planned to file suit.

"Le Pen, Megret, out of Marseille!" the demonstrators chanted. Le Pen favours sending home three million immigrants in an extreme strategy that has gained him popularity at a time of record unemployment in France.
Catherine Megret's victory in Vitrolles last month handed the Front control of its fourth town hall in France and shocked mainstream parties ahead of National Assembly elections in a year's time.

Separately in Paris, police clashed with demonstrators at the end of a protest rally outside the Senate, where Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre earlier defended a controversial bill to crack down on illegal immigration.

France Info radio said 15 people were detained and that some cars were damaged. About 4,000 people, according to police figures, took part in the earlier rally outside the Senate where the bill, already approved by the lower house, was having a final reading.

In the south-western city of Toulouse, at least 1,000 people marched behind a banner denouncing a "racist government" in France. The marches were tiny compared to a protest by an estimated 100,000 in Paris on February 22 against the bill.

"Illegal immigration is too serious a threat for our country as for all developed countries for us not to address it head on, without illusions," Debre said, adding that did not mean a lack of humanity.

"Let us ignore the slanders and the bad taste comparisons," he said. "Let us simply and firmly remind the cartoonists that the France of today is neither the French state of Vichy nor the Greek tyranny of Creon but a democracy founded on the respect of law."

The bill would tighten police powers to monitor immigrants in France as well as closing loopholes in existing 1993 legislation. The bill, for instance, makes it easier to carry out fingerprinting or retaining passports.
